name: TheWhiteKnight
summary: TheWhiteKnight is a web app called CareerOS that helps a job seeker manage a job search. It keeps a career profile, lets the user add job postings by link, file, photo or text, and scores how well each job fits. It uses AI to write resumes, cover letters, outreach messages and answers to application questions. It also scans job boards, suggests target companies, finds contacts at those companies, and plans skills to build. Most personal data is kept in the browser, while accounts and invite codes are kept in an online database.
who_its_for: A job seeker who wants one place to track applications and have AI draft their materials. Sign-up needs an invite code, so it looks like a private tool for a small group.
how_it_runs: It is a Next.js web app that is built and deployed through Vercel, with a GitHub Pages workflow also present (which of the two is the real live setup is unclear). Server routes call AI providers and outside services using keys from the settings file, and the pages run in the browser.

areas.name: app/api
areas.summary: The server routes behind the app. They handle login and sign-up, admin invites, AI writing and scoring, reading uploaded files and web pages, job scanning, contact search and sending email.
areas.why: This is where the AI and outside services are actually called, so most of the real work happens here.
areas.debug_tips: If a feature fails, find the matching route and check that its API key is set. The health route is a quick test that the AI is responding. The scoring route was only partly reviewed.

areas.name: lib
areas.summary: Shared helper code. It covers the AI gateway, clients for Adzuna, Apollo, Exa and Resend, login tokens, the database, prompts, scoring, and browser storage for profile, applications, contacts and skills.
areas.why: Both the pages and the server routes rely on these helpers, so a change here affects many features.
areas.debug_tips: Missing data after a reload usually points to the browser storage files (store, profile, contacts-store). Login problems point to session.ts or kv.ts. Some files, such as integration-settings.ts and resend-client.ts, were only partly seen.

areas.name: app
areas.summary: The main screens and shared pieces: home list, job ingest, companies, contacts, config, settings, skills, onboarding, login, register, plus the layout, styles and notification inbox.
areas.why: This is everything the user sees and clicks.
areas.debug_tips: Check the page file for the screen with the problem, then follow it to the API route it calls. Config shows values written in the code, not saved ones. Some pages (home, profile) were only partly reviewed.

areas.name: (root files)
areas.summary: Project setup files: the package list, build and TypeScript settings, the login-checking middleware, the Vercel settings, an example settings file and a sync script.
areas.why: They decide how the app is built, started and protected.
areas.debug_tips: Build errors usually trace to package.json, next.config.js or tsconfig.json. Being sent to the login page unexpectedly points to middleware.ts.

areas.name: .github
areas.summary: Automated GitHub jobs. One deploys the site to GitHub Pages, one does a one-time project bootstrap, and one unzips a persona pack and commits it.
areas.why: They publish the site and load starter content without manual steps.
areas.debug_tips: Open the Actions tab on GitHub and read the failing job's log. The two zip-based jobs expect specific files in the repository root.

areas.name: app/application
areas.summary: The screen for one application: status, notes, AI document generation and printable export. A small redirect page moves visitors from a slug address to this screen.
areas.why: This is where the user works on a specific job.
areas.debug_tips: If a link opens the wrong or blank application, check the slug redirect files first. If generation fails, look at the generate route.

areas.name: app/persona
areas.summary: A page that reads persona notes files from disk and shows them in a browser viewer.
areas.why: It lets the user read the persona material that guides the writing.
areas.debug_tips: If files do not appear, check the persona API route and the folder it reads. Both files here were only partly visible.

areas.name: app/profile
areas.summary: Pages to view the career profile and to edit it across eight tabs with automatic saving.
areas.why: The profile feeds the scoring and all the AI-written documents.
areas.debug_tips: If edits vanish, check browser storage in lib/profile.ts. The view page was only partly reviewed.

areas.name: app/admin
areas.summary: A one-time screen where the owner creates the admin account using a setup secret.
areas.why: It is the first step to get an admin who can issue invite codes.
areas.debug_tips: If setup is rejected, check that the setup secret in the server settings matches what was typed.

areas.name: app/applications
areas.summary: The list of all saved applications, sorted by score, with a button to add a new job.
areas.why: It is the main overview of the job search.
areas.debug_tips: If an application is missing, check browser storage in lib/store.ts, since data is saved per browser.

areas.name: app/batch
areas.summary: A screen for running several job postings through the pipeline at once. Only its setup was reviewed, so its full behavior is unclear.
areas.why: It saves time when many postings need scoring.
areas.debug_tips: Look at lib/batch-runner.ts and the score route, since the runner does the scoring work.

readiness.summary: Top fixes: write a real README with setup, run and deploy steps; add automated tests with a test script; and add logging plus error tracking, with a git history secret scan and a dependency audit as close follow-ups.

checks.question: Does the app build and start with one documented command?
checks.evidence: `package.json` defines `dev`, `build` and `start` scripts for Next.js, but the README is only a title line (`# TheWhiteKnight`) and documents no command. Build was not run.
checks.next_step: Add a Quick start section to `README.md` with install, env setup and `npm run dev`.

checks.question: Are there automated tests, and do they pass?
checks.evidence: No real tests found. The 2 'test files' matched are `docs/spec/.gitkeep` and `docs/spec/tasks/.gitkeep`, and `package.json` has no test script. Tests were not run.
checks.next_step: Add a test runner and a `test` script, then write tests for the core flows.

checks.question: When something goes wrong, does the app show a clear message instead of crashing or failing silently?
checks.evidence: Not checked: error handling needs code reading and running the app. Static scan found 0 swallowed errors, which is not proof of clear user-facing messages.
checks.next_step: Review API routes and add error boundaries (`error.tsx`) with clear messages.

checks.question: Does it check what people type or upload before using it?
checks.evidence: 10 input validation matches in 6 files, so some checking exists, but coverage across all inputs and uploads is not confirmed.
checks.next_step: List every form and API route and confirm each uses schema validation (for example zod).

checks.question: Are passwords and API keys kept out of the code and out of git history?
checks.evidence: Only `.env.example` is tracked, `.gitignore` mentions `.env`, and 0 secret-like strings in HEAD. Git history was not scanned.
checks.next_step: Run a history scan (gitleaks or trufflehog) and rotate any key that shows up.

checks.question: Can only the right people see and change things (sign-in and permissions)?
checks.evidence: 84 auth/session/permission matches in 18 files suggest sign-in logic exists, but whether every route and data access is protected is not verified.
checks.next_step: Audit each route and API handler for an auth check and add tests for unauthorized access.

checks.question: Is important data backed up, and are database changes made through migrations?
checks.evidence: No migrations folders found and no backup configuration in the evidence.
checks.next_step: If a database is used, adopt a migration tool and document a backup and restore routine; if not, state that in the docs.

checks.question: Are third-party packages reasonably up to date and free of known security problems?
checks.evidence: Not checked: dependency audit was not run. `package-lock.json` exists, which allows a reproducible audit.
checks.next_step: Run `npm audit` and `npm outdated`, and consider enabling Dependabot.

checks.question: If it breaks while people use it, will logs or alerts show what happened?
checks.evidence: Only 1 logging match in 1 file, and no monitoring or alerting config is visible.
checks.next_step: Add structured logging on server routes and an error tracker such as Sentry.

checks.question: Does it stay fast with realistic amounts of data and users?
checks.evidence: Not checked: performance needs running the app with realistic data. No load testing or caching evidence in the static scan.
checks.next_step: Profile key pages and queries with realistic data and add caching or pagination where needed.

checks.question: Is there a written, repeatable way to deploy it and to roll back a bad release?
checks.evidence: `.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml` and `vercel.json` exist, so deploys are automated, but there is no written deploy or rollback procedure, and two deploy targets (Pages and Vercel) may confuse.
checks.next_step: Document the chosen deploy path and rollback steps (for example Vercel redeploy of a previous build) in `README.md`.

checks.question: Could someone new run it and understand it from the docs alone?
checks.evidence: `README.md` contains only the project title. The other docs are agent skill files under `.agent/` and `.claude/`, which are not onboarding documentation.
checks.next_step: Write a README covering purpose, setup, env variables from `.env.example`, run, and deploy.

readiness.method: Static evidence only; tests, build and audit were not run in this pass.

debug_playbook.symptom: Cannot log in or sign up
steps: Check that the signing secret and Redis database link are set as in .env.example.
Confirm the invite code exists and is unused.
If you keep landing on the login page, review middleware.ts.

debug_playbook.symptom: AI writing, scoring or parsing fails
steps: Open the health route to see whether the AI responds and which provider is used.
Check the AI key in the server settings or in the Settings page.
Then read the specific route that failed.

debug_playbook.symptom: Saved applications, profile or contacts disappear
steps: Remember this data lives in the browser, so a different browser or cleared data shows nothing.
Check browser storage for the saved entries.
Review the store file for the data type that is missing.

debug_playbook.symptom: Job scan or contact search returns nothing
steps: Check that the Adzuna, Apollo or Exa keys are entered in Settings or the server settings.
Look at the matching client file for the error it returns.
Confirm the company list in app/companies/page.tsx is not empty.

debug_playbook.symptom: Site does not build or deploy
steps: Read the failed job log in GitHub Actions or Vercel.
Check the build command in package.json and vercel.json.
It is unclear whether GitHub Pages or Vercel is the main host, so confirm which one is in use.

glossary.meaning: The app's product name, seen in the layout and workflows.
The web framework the app is built with.
A server-side address the pages call to do work such as writing or scoring.
A single-use code an admin creates so a new person can register.
Notes files describing the candidate that guide the AI writing.
A default job group with title words, keywords and weights used to sort jobs.
Applicant tracking system, software employers use to read resumes.
The online database that holds accounts and invite codes.
A check that runs before each request and sends logged-out visitors to login.
